paraphrase: King Paesi holds that soul and body are one (tajjīva-taccharīra) and gives his proofs: his wicked grandfather, who should be in hell, never came to warn him; his pious grandmother never came from heaven; a thief shut in a sealed iron jar died without any hole appearing for the soul to leave, and worms later appeared in a sealed corpse without any hole for souls to enter; a man weighed alive and dead weighed the same; a man cut into pieces showed no soul.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Rājapraśnīya (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory. Parallel to DN 23.

paraphrase: Kesi answers each proof with a simile — the hell-bound grandfather is held like a prisoner, the heavenly grandmother is detained by delight, sound escapes a sealed chamber without a hole, a filled and an empty skin weigh the same, and the woodcutter who chopped up the fire-sticks to find the fire found none — until the king accepts the lay vows.
speaker: Kesi Kumāra
notes: From memory; the order of similes is uncertain.

paraphrase: The god Sūryābha comes from his celestial palace to honour Mahāvīra and stages a divine dance; the text describes his palace, in which he worships the images of the Jinas with water, sandal, flowers, incense and lamps.
notes: The Mūrtipūjakas' prime canonical example of image worship; Sthānakavāsīs read it as the conduct of gods, not an injunction for humans.
